1.35.0.en: Father Dorotheus v Fear the Lord and keep His commandments, which strengthen you in all your affairs, so that there is none like your works... Do not fear Satan if you fear the Lord, for your fear of God gives you authority over Satan [38].

1.35.1.en: Hermas St. Clement of Alexandria sees that the Lord often speaks and threatens before He disciplines, so that man may turn back from his evil.

1.36.0.en: v The Lord often speaks before He carries out the work (the discipline). He says: "I will spend My arrows upon them; they shall be burnt with hunger, and devoured with burning heat, and with bitter destruction. I will also send the teeth of beasts upon them, with the poison of serpents of the earth. The sword without, and terror within, shall destroy" (Deut 32:23-25). This does not mean that the Divine Spirit becomes angry, as some suppose. He often shows restraint along with encouragement, and shows us what we ought to do. He uses this effective means, which lies in stirring up fear in us, so that we do not commit sin [39].

1.36.1.en: St. Clement of Alexandria Unjust anger cannot be justified, for the sure effect of anger causes its downfall [19].

1.37.0.en: v In truth, just as madmen and fools do not notice this when they cast themselves into the abyss, so it is with those who lose their gentleness and are struck by anger. This is why the wise man, who wishes to expose the destruction of this intoxication (anger), says: "The wrath of man turns the scale of the balance to his own destruction." Observe how he binds himself in slavery to the work of this passion, destructive in its weight [40].

1.37.1.en: v Anger is a ravening beast, a violent and raging beast. Let us then prescribe for ourselves a soothing draught taken from Holy Scripture, and say: "Why (how) is he proud who is dust and ashes?" (Sir 10:9), the weight of his anger destroys him (cf. Sir 1:19)... Nothing is more shameful, nothing is uglier than a face inflamed with anger. When you stir up mud, you smell a foul odor. And when a soul is disturbed by passion, it becomes exceedingly foul [41].

1.37.2.en: v The passion of anger is ravenous, fiercer than any flame. For this reason we need to hasten very quickly to prevent the flame, and not allow it to blaze up on high. For this sickness becomes the cause of many evils. It brings down whole houses, dissolves old friendships, and causes calamities that cannot be remedied in a short time. It was said: "The wrath of man turns the scale of the balance to his own destruction" [42].

1.37.3.en: St. John Chrysostom The long-suffering man bears patiently until the right time, and afterward joy returns to him with power [20].

1.37.4.en: Ben Sirach distinguishes between a man who is wronged and so becomes angry and rages, and another who falls under wrong and endures with long-suffering. The first, although his anger rests on a wrong that has befallen him, is burdened by his own anger, and so he falls, even if he thinks he is justifying himself. The second endures for a time in silence, and then joy returns to him, and many bear witness for him while he is silent and does not defend himself.

1.37.5.en: He holds back his words until the right time, and the lips of many tell of his understanding [21].

1.38.0.en: 31 In the treasures of wisdom are the parables of knowledge, 32 but to the sinner the worship of God is an abomination. 33 My son, if you desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and the Lord will give her to you. 34 For wisdom and instruction are the fear of the Lord, and that which pleases Him 35 is faith and meekness, and He will fill him who has them with treasures. 36 Do not disobey the fear of the Lord, and do not come to Him with a double heart. 37 Be not a hypocrite in the sight of men, and keep watch over your lips. 38 Exalt not yourself, lest you fall, and bring dishonor upon your soul, 39 and the Lord reveal your secrets, and cast you down in the midst of the congregation, 40 because you came not to the fear of the Lord, but your heart is full of deceit.

1.38.1.en: In the treasures of wisdom are the parables of knowledge, but godliness is an abomination to the sinner [22].

1.38.2.en: If godliness is an abomination to the sinner, how much more can the enemy of good, the devil, not bear it, and so he rages against the godly; yet he has no authority to harm them.

1.38.3.en: v If (the demons) had authority, they would not hesitate to use it, but would practice evil at once, since this is their aim, especially against us.

1.38.4.en: Behold, we are gathered together speaking against them, and they know it, that the more we advance, the weaker they become. If they had authority, they would not have allowed any of us Christians to live, for the service of God is an abomination to the sinner (cf. Sir 1:22). But since they have no authority, they harm themselves, for they cannot carry out anything of what they threaten. This obliges us not to fear them [43].

1.38.5.en: St. Athanasius the Apostolic If you desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and the Lord will give her to you [23].

1.38.6.en: The philosophy discovered by the Gentiles is the product of human understanding, but Holy Scripture proclaims that understanding is from God Himself, who gives it to him who believes in His commandments.

1.38.7.en: v Do not forsake the commandment of the Lord, but keep what you have received, neither adding to it nor taking away from it [44].

1.38.8.en: The Didache (the Teaching of the Twelve Disciples)

1.38.9.en: v I have been absorbed in the commandments that You gave me, and meditated on them with wisdom; I believed in them until I kept them.

1.38.10.en: Grant me, then, wisdom by teaching me goodness, discipline and knowledge.

1.38.11.en: This petition agrees with the saying: "My son, if you desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and the Lord will give her to you" (cf. Sir 1:23).

1.38.12.en: St. Didymus the Blind v The (first) Psalm draws for us the way of virtue with knowledge and skill. Turning away from evil is the beginning of good. If you ask from the beginning for the perfection of virtue, you will draw back before you start; but the Psalm prepares the way for us to face it with courage.

1.38.13.en: And I believe that growth in the love of God is like the ladder that the blessed Jacob once saw, which was on the earth on one side and on the other side was reaching toward the life of virtue, where a man begins by climbing the first rungs of the ladder, and after that rises to a higher rung with deliberation and patience, until he reaches what human nature can attain.

1.38.14.en: So, by climbing the first rungs of the ladder, we rise above the earth, to live the life that God wills for us.

1.38.15.en: And the beginning of progress is to keep away from evil, where such keeping away is easy, as in: "You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal" (Ex 20:13-15); this does not require any positive work. But when we are required to keep that commandment: "Love your neighbor as yourself," "Sell what you have and give to the poor" (Mt 19:21), "Whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two" (Mt 5:41), these works are done by the wrestler who has tested his strength by divine wisdom, who through small works leads us to perfection.

1.38.16.en: For he sets before us three things that we must avoid: walking in the counsel of the wicked, standing in the way of sinners, and sitting in the seat of the scornful.

1.38.17.en: This order begins with making the decision and then carrying out the beginning, here in pure thought. For the foundation of the works of the flesh springs from purity of heart; adultery begins in the lustful soul and ends in adultery of the body. Therefore the Lord said: "That which defiles a man comes out of the heart" (cf. Mt 15:18) [45].

1.38.18.en: St. Basil the Great Origen sees that wisdom begins with upright conduct, or keeping the divine commandment.

1.38.19.en: v If anyone meditates in the law of the Lord day and night (Ps 1:2), and is like the mouth of the righteous that speaks wisdom (Ps 37:30), he will be able to ask with care and find. So it will be, on condition that he asks in a sound manner, and by his asking knocks at the door of wisdom, to ask God to open it to him, and is made worthy to receive by the Holy Spirit the word of wisdom and the word of knowledge, and becomes a companion of the wisdom of Solomon [46].

1.38.20.en: v "I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded" (Prov 1:24). It is reasonable that he said that He (God) stretches out His words in his heart (the heart of Solomon)... because God gave him a large heart.

1.38.21.en: He is able to explain, in brief, what is stated in the mysteries, within the broad, harmonious and confirmed teachings of Holy Scripture, since he has a large heart.

1.38.22.en: Therefore, in agreement with the teachings of the wise Solomon, it is necessary for the person who desires to know wisdom to begin with training in conduct, so that he may understand what is written: "Do you long for wisdom? Keep the commandments, and it will be given to you by God" [47].

1.38.23.en: Origen v Wisdom is good; it fills with joy those who possess her, and brings down those who do not practice (the commandments).

1.38.24.en: But what does Holy Scripture say? The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (cf. Sir 1:12). Who does not love to reign? And in the Psalms there is the counsel of the Spirit: "Now therefore, O you kings, be wise; be instructed, you judges of the earth. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling." This is the reason for Paul's saying: "Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling" (Phil 2:12). And we read: "If you desire wisdom, observe justice, and the Lord will grant her to you [48]."

1.38.25.en: v You must order your life by the commandments of God, which we receive to help us walk the good life, beginning with godly fear, for "the fear of the Lord is the head of wisdom" (Prov 1:7), while human pride breaks and weakens [49].

1.38.26.en: The commandments are those that concern the good, that is, bring the good; and the good is faith without doubt. Hence wisdom is the reward of pure faith. And the reward will be what eye has not seen [50].

1.38.27.en: St. Augustine v People are commonly called "wise," with a misuse of the word "wise." For the wise are not those who study the sayings and writings of the early wise Fathers, but those whose souls are rational, able to distinguish between what is good and what is evil. They avoid what is evil and harmful to the soul, and wisely take care of what is good and profitable to the soul and practice it with great thanksgiving to God. These alone are truly those whom we should call "wise" [51].

1.38.28.en: St. Anthony the Great v The knowledge of goodness is not enough for blessedness for him who does not put goodness into practice; true godliness toward God is the beginning of knowledge [52].

1.38.29.en: St. Didymus the Blind For the fear of the Lord is wisdom and instruction, and that which pleases Him is faith and meekness [24].

1.38.30.en: v In truth the divinity is not angry, as some suppose; rather, when God uses many threats, He does this as an appeal, showing mankind the things that will come to pass. These are measures that are certainly good; He plants fear to keep us from sin. "The fear of the Lord drives away sin, and he who has no fear cannot be justified." The punishment that God imposes is not from anger but from justice; and he who neglects justice makes no progress [53].

1.38.31.en: St. Clement of Alexandria Do not disobey the fear of the Lord, and do not come to Him with a double heart [25].

1.38.32.en: An undivided mind: to enjoy the holy fear of the Lord, which gives wisdom, it is fitting for the believer to keep the divine commandments, for they support his faith in God, and also grant him to be adorned with meekness, so that he does not fall into arrogance even toward unbelievers [27]. And on the other hand, he clings to God with all his heart, without duplicity.

1.38.33.en: As he speaks of wisdom and its connection with the divine commandment, he calls us to the life of simplicity as the key to obedience to the commandment, warning us against the double heart. If simplicity directs our hearts to the way of truth without deviation, the double heart makes man lose his aim, so that he gives an hour to the Lord and an hour to amusement and temporal pleasures.

1.38.34.en: As St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, speaks of the virtues, he puts simplicity of heart first, which is the opposite of duplicity of heart, saying:

1.38.35.en: v Concerning the elements of virtue, which kind of them it is fitting to regard as the greatest, and which of them we need to practice more than the others, this is their order; these things cannot be put into words. For they all have the same dignity, and lead the one who practices them to the heights by way of each one of them.

1.38.36.en: For simplicity opens the way to obedience, and obedience to faith, and faith to hope, and hope to righteousness (justice), and righteousness to service, and service to humility. By this is achieved the kindness that leads to grace, and grace to love, and love to prayer. Thus every virtue depends on the other virtues. And the virtues lead us to the summit of what we desire. Just as the crown of evil leads its friends to ever-increasing evil... Besides this, it is necessary for us to continue steadfastly in prayer (Rom 12:12). For prayer is like the leader of the chorus of the virtues [54].

1.38.37.en: St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa Let us follow God with our whole being, or with all our heart and all our mind: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind" (Lk 10:27).

1.38.38.en: v These alone receive within them the greatness of the commandment and its priority: not only do they love the Lord their God, but they set themselves to accomplish this by three conditions; that is, with all their heart they hold within them the perfection of this love, its thoughts and its works; and with all their soul, that is, they are ready to give it up for the service of God who created all things, when the spreading of His word requires it; for God is loved with all the soul when no part of the soul is held back outside the keeping of the faith; and they love Him with all the mind, so that they think of nothing and speak of nothing but the divine things [55].

1.38.39.en: Origen v I believe that the wise man counsels divided persons, likening them to those who approach the way of God, when he says: "Do not come to the Lord with two hearts," but draw near to His way as one who sows and another who reaps [56].

1.38.40.en: St. Isaac the Syrian v The virtuous life is truly the source and root of wisdom, just as iniquity has folly as its source. I say this because the boaster and the slave of lust is taken captive by these vices as the fruit of lack of wisdom... Every sin begins with a lack of wisdom, just as the virtuous person who fears God is the wisest of all. For this reason the wise man says: "The fear of the Lord is the head of wisdom" (Prov 1:7). If the fear of the Lord is to be wise, and the evildoer does not possess this fear, then he is truly stripped of wisdom, and he who is deprived of wisdom is truly the most foolish of all [57].

1.38.41.en: St. John Chrysostom v It is fitting for the Christian to think thus of his heavenly calling, and that his life be worthy of the gospel of Christ (Phil 1:27). It is fitting that the Christian not be of a double mind (Lk 12:29), nor be distracted from remembering God and His purposes and His judgments [58].

1.38.42.en: St. Basil the Great Be not a hypocrite in the sight of men, and keep watch over your lips [26].

1.38.43.en: It was said of the pride of the hypocrite that it lifts him up as if to heaven; with his arrogant thought he seems as one who leads himself to the heavenly life. In hypocrisy he thinks that his head has reached the clouds, for he thinks that his thinking mind is equal to the merits of the saints who went before him.

1.38.44.en: v Hypocrisy is hateful to God and abhorred by men; it brings no reward, and is of no use at all for the salvation of the soul, but rather destroys it. If someone flees into hypocrisy so that his matter may not be discovered, it is only for a time, for it does not last long; rather, everything is revealed, and brings shame upon its owner. Thus he is like an ugly woman whose outward adornment, put on her by artificial means, is stripped from her. Hypocrisy, then, is foreign to the saints, since it is impossible for anything of what we do or say to escape the eyes of the divinity, for it was said: "There is nothing covered that shall not be revealed, neither hid that shall not be known" (Lk 12:2). If all our words and works will be revealed on the day of judgment, then hypocrisy is wearisome and without profit. It is fitting for us to be proved as true worshippers who serve God with sincere and open countenances [59].

1.38.45.en: St. Cyril the Great v There may be one who gives his alms before men yet avoids making a show of it, and there is also one who does not give it before men yet boasts of it in secret. For God does not reward almsgiving according to how it is done, whether before men or not, but according to the intention of the one who does it [60].

1.38.46.en: v Everyone sees the thief, "hypocrisy," carrying everything before his eyes, and he rejoices in it! What a new kind of robbery, which attracts people and delights them while they are being robbed! [61]

1.38.47.en: St. John Chrysostom v What is the place of the hypocrite (Job 20:9) but the heart of his flatterers? For he rests in the place where he finds those who love him... But as long as he lives, he does not cease to teach his followers the same things that he practices, and through the boldness of his sinful way he begets others also in the likeness of his own vain deceit.

1.38.48.en: v Hypocrites appear fruitful and green in the eyes of their fellow creatures, but in the sight of the hidden Judge they appear fruitless and withered.

1.38.50.en: Do not exalt yourself, lest you fall, and bring dishonor upon your soul.

1.38.51.en: And the Lord will reveal your secrets, and strike you down in the midst of the congregation, because you truly did not come to the fear of the Lord, and your heart is full of deceit [27].

1.38.52.en: Wisdom is a free gift that He offers to the humble; He offers it without partiality, and gives it to those who enjoy the fear of the Lord and take care to keep His commandments [27].

1.38.53.en: v Hate greatness, for it is the fruit full of death.

1.38.54.en: For Adam ate of it in Eden, and it gave him death.

1.38.55.en: And by it Satan fell from the beginning. By it the house of Adam fell from Paradise.

1.38.56.en: There is nothing with God so vile and hateful as the love of greatness, and him who exalts himself in pride.

1.38.57.en: St. Jacob of Serugh v Observe these proud and reckless people; observe the ox as it is prepared for slaughter, left to roam in freedom, destroying what it wishes, until the day of its slaughter... Holy Scripture points to it in another place as a sacrifice, and that it is left to an evil freedom (Prov 7:22) [62].

1.38.58.en: St. Augustine v Satan fell from his heavenly rank because of his pride; therefore he always does all he can to make fall all who wish to advance toward God with all their hearts, using the same means by which he himself fell, I mean greatness and the love of vainglory. By this and the like he fights us, in the hope of drawing us away from God...

1.38.59.en: What moved our Lord Jesus Christ to lay aside His garments, and gird Himself with a towel, and pour water into a basin, and wash the feet of those who were beneath Him (Jn 13:4 etc.), if not to teach us humility?! He showed us humility by the example He gave. Therefore those who wish to return to their first rank will not be able to do so except by humility. For pride is the cause of the fall from heaven in the beginning.

1.38.60.en: And so he who lacks deep humility, from all the heart and mind and spirit and body, does not inherit the Kingdom of God [63].

1.38.61.en: v Many have lived a long time as monks and virgins, and have not learned how to acquire purity. This is because they despise the teaching of their fathers and follow the desires of their own hearts. Therefore the evil spirits that destroy souls gained mastery over them, wounding them night and day with their unseen arrows, and giving them peace nowhere; rather they occupy their hearts now with pride, and now with vainglory and evil jealousy and slander and anger and fury and quarrels and many other passions. These have their portion with the five foolish virgins, for they passed their time in folly, and did not bridle their tongues, nor keep their eyes pure, nor keep their bodies from lusts or their hearts from impurities and the like [64].

1.38.62.en: St. Anthony the Great Inspired by Sirach 1

1.39.s.en: Let me possess You, O wisdom of the eternal God!

1.39.0.en: v You are the wisdom of God, Creator of heaven and earth!

1.39.1.en: You are the wise One, greatly to be feared, sitting upon Your throne!

1.39.2.en: Who, of the heavenly orders or of men, can search out the mysteries of Your creation?!

1.39.3.en: Who can search out Your nature?

1.39.4.en: You are the wisdom of God; You came down to me that I might possess You, and become wise through You.

1.39.5.en: You are the Giver of wisdom and of every blessing; You have become a gift to me. I possess You within me and I cherish You!

1.39.6.en: v You gave me reason together with freedom of will so that I might contemplate the works of Your love; but when I stood helpless, You came down to me to dwell in my depths!

1.39.7.en: You came down to me to carry me in Yourself, and to prepare for me a place in Your heavens.

1.39.8.en: I meet You face to face, and my insight remains in amazement.

1.39.9.en: I depart to Paradise, and enjoy the eternal glories and their mysteries, without ceasing!

1.39.10.en: v My soul blesses You, who have given me the instinct of holy fear.

1.39.11.en: As I come to know You, Your holy fear is fixed in me, and my depths are glorified by Your dwelling in them.

1.39.12.en: I glory in You, my joy and the gladness of my heart!

1.39.13.en: Your fear leads me on the journey of my sojourn until the day of my departure from the world.

1.39.14.en: Your fear joins me to the orders of the heavenly ones, and I praise You with them with fear and trembling.

1.39.15.en: Your fear turns the dry wilderness of my heart into a paradise full of the fruit of the Spirit.

1.39.16.en: Your fear cleanses me from the fear of the devil and the fear of men!

1.39.17.en: By Your fear I defy the devil and all his forces and all his works, so that no evil thought can steal into me, nor idle word, nor wicked conduct!

1.39.18.en: Your fear is a tree of life, whose branches extend to my emotions and senses and words and conduct.

1.39.19.en: I pluck from it, and I am sanctified within and without.

1.39.20.en: I pluck from it Your love, and I love all mankind, even those who oppose me!

1.39.21.en: v You made with me a wonderful covenant of love, which You recorded in Your holy book.

1.39.22.en: You gave me Your book to meditate in, and my soul is filled with Your sweetness!

1.39.23.en: Your commandments are the precious jewelry that adorns my soul!

1.39.24.en: Your commandments prepare me for the eternal wedding.

1.39.25.en: My soul sits as a queen adorned with Your commandments, and the heavenly ones marvel at her!

1.39.26.en: For every perfection I have seen an end, but Your commandments are exceedingly broad.

1.39.27.en: Since You presented Yourself to me as a heavenly friend, You gave me Your wisdom and Your fear and Your commandment!

1.39.28.en: How can I suffer isolation, when You accompany me throughout the journey of my sojourn?

1.39.29.en: How can I complain of my poverty and need, when I am rich in You!

1.39.30.en: v Glory to You for Your companionship with me, so that I turn neither to the right nor to the left.

1.39.31.en: My heart will not know duplicity, for it is in Your hand.

1.39.32.en: Your love fills my whole heart, so the devil will find no place in it!

1.39.33.en: Glory to You, O All-wise, Giver of holy fear, and Your commandment full of sweetness!

1.39.34.en: Appendix to Sirach 1 The fear of the Lord The fear of the Lord is manifested in obedience to His commandments, and he who keeps His commandments enjoys inner glory, and lives in the joy and gladness of the Spirit, and receives a crown of rejoicing. Some claim that God's commandments and judgments humiliate man, because they have not experienced the truth of the commandments, which restore to man the image of God so that he becomes in His likeness, and so lives in joy.

1.39.35.en: The goal of the commandment is that God may dwell in us and in our midst (Zech 2:5). Therefore the fear of the Lord is glory and pride and gladness and a crown of rejoicing.

1.39.36.en: "The fear of the Lord was created with the faithful in the womb" [12]. Thus the parents' care for their children begins before their birth. For when Zacharias the priest and Elizabeth were sanctified, and St. Mary visited them and brought the incarnate Word, the child John leaped and ran rejoicing in the Lord, and enjoyed the fear of the Lord while still in the womb.

1.39.37.en: a. There is a relation between wisdom and the fear of the Lord. Both bring happiness and blessing. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom and its fulfillment and its crown [12, 16, 18].

1.39.38.en: b. Wisdom is a mother and bride to him who fears the Lord: "She will meet him as a mother, and receive him as a wife married in her youth" (15:2).

1.39.39.en: c. The eyes of the Lord are upon him who fears the Lord: "And He knows every work of man" (15:19).

1.39.40.en: d. Those who fear the Lord are filled with blessings and hope: "The fear of the Lord is like a paradise of blessing" (40:27).

1.39.41.en: e. Those who fear the Lord and the word of God: "They that fear the Lord will not disobey His words" (2:15).

1.39.42.en: The possibilities of him who fears the Lord: "He that fears the Lord shall fear nothing, and shall not be afraid, for He is his hope" (34:14). "There shall no evil happen to him that fears the Lord; but in temptation He (the Lord) will deliver him again and again. A wise man hates not the law, but he that makes a show of keeping it is like a boat in a storm. A man of understanding trusts in the law, and the law is faithful to him, for it is a divine revelation" (33:1-3).

1.39.43.en: f. The honor of him who fears the Lord: "What seed is honorable? They that fear the Lord" (10:19).

1.39.44.en: g. The fear of the Lord is the pride of the elders: "Much experience is the crown of old men, and the fear of the Lord is their glory" (25:6).

1.39.45.en: h. The fear of the Lord surpasses every good: "The fear of the Lord surpasses all things" (25:11).

1.39.46.en: i. A good wife is a gift to those who fear the Lord: "A good wife is a great portion, and shall be given to him that fears the Lord" (26:3; cf. 27:3).

1.40.s.en: Between those who fear the Lord and the wicked

1.40.0.en: "He that fears the Lord will receive instruction, and they that seek Him early shall find favor. He that seeks the law shall be filled with it, but the hypocrite will stumble at it. They that fear the Lord shall find judgment, and shall kindle righteous works as a light. A sinful man will not be reproved, but finds an excuse according to his will" (32:14-17).

1.41.s.en: The fear of the Lord and economic life

1.41.0.en: 1. He speaks to us of riches and poverty; riches are good for him who is holy, and poverty is hateful in the mind of the wicked (cf. 13:23). Riches give a man authority and self-confidence, but not like the fear of the Lord and good counsel.

1.41.1.en: "Gold and silver make the foot stand sure, but counsel is esteemed above them both. Riches and strength lift up the heart, but the fear of the Lord is above them both. There is no loss in the fear of the Lord, and it needs not to seek help" (40:25-26). 2. The rich and the poor: "The rich man does wrong, and yet he proves himself the one wronged, while the poor man is wronged, and is obliged to apologize" (13:3).

1.41.2.en: He warns us of the importance of work in the spiritual and economic life even to old age: "Hate not laborious work, especially husbandry, which the Most High has created... Have you cattle? Look to them" (cf. 7:15, 22). "My son, lead not a beggar's life; for it is better to die than to beg. When a man looks to the table of another, his living is not to be counted for a life. He loses his self-respect by another man's food, but a man who is wise and well instructed will guard against it. In the mouth of the shameless begging is sweet, but in his belly there burns a fire" (cf. 40:28-30). 3. He warns us of just weights and measures: "A merchant will hardly keep himself from doing wrong, and a huckster shall not be freed from sin" (cf. 26:20). 4. True wisdom and work without planning: "Strive not in a matter that concerns you not, and sit not with sinners in their judgment. My son, meddle not with many matters, for if you multiply them, you shall not go unpunished; and if you pursue them, you shall not overtake them, nor escape by fleeing. There is one that labors, and takes pains, and makes haste, and is so much the more in want" (cf. 11:9-11). 5. The right use of money: "Watching for riches consumes the flesh, and the care of it takes away sleep... The rich man toils in gathering money together, and when he rests, he is filled with his delicacies. The poor man toils in lack of living, and when he rests, he becomes needy. He that loves gold shall not be justified, and he that follows corruption shall be filled with it... It is a stumbling block to them that sacrifice their lives to it, and every fool shall be taken by it. Blessed is the rich man that is found without blemish, and has not gone after gold" (cf. 31:1, 3-5, 7-8).

1.42.s.en: Let us begin with the primary fear

1.42.0.en: v No one can attain to perfect fear unless he first has the primary fear. For the wise Ben Sirach says: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord... the crown (head) of wisdom is the fear of God" (Sirach 1:12, 16), meaning by the word "head" the primary fear, which is followed by the perfect fear of the saints.

1.42.1.en: The primary fear depends on the state of our spirit, and it keeps the soul from every fall, for it was said that by the fear of the Lord everyone departs from evil. But the man who is rid of evil because of his fear of punishment is like a slave who fears his master, and gradually he begins to do good willingly.

1.42.2.en: In the beginning he works as a hired servant who awaits his wages for his good work. If he continues thus, avoiding evil because of fear like a slave, doing good in the hope of receiving the reward like a hired servant, then he abides in doing good and gains a particular taste for spiritual good, so that he no longer wishes to be separated from it. Then he reaches the work of a son, and loves good for the sake of good itself; and though he fears, he works because he loves. This is the great, perfect fear.

1.43.s.en: The fear of the Lord and the ladder of the life of faith

1.43.0.en: St. Philoxenus presents to us the ladder of the practical life of faith, beginning with its three steps: faith, simplicity and the fear of the Lord. There is no fellowship with God without faith, and faith cannot stand except through the simplicity that God gave to the soul so that it might meet Him as a simple child who believes in his father and clings to him. This simplicity that begets faith is what preserves it, so that the soul, by the grace of God, continues firm in its faith.

1.43.1.en: Through this faith the soul enjoys the fear of the Lord. It believes in Him and perceives His greatness, and so it fears Him, honors Him, and keeps His commandments. Faith, then, begets "the fear of the Lord"; so the believing man keeps the commandment and obeys it out of fear of punishment... and as he grows by grace he obeys the commandment as a son who fears to wound his father's feelings... He fears that his nature, which he holds in the image of his God and Savior, may be disfigured.
